briefing:
The headline Airfare Price Index (APIx) registered at 100.74 for the reporting period of September 14, 2026, marking a modest overall increase of 0.74% above the baseline reference period. This reflects a slightly inflationary aggregate trend across key domestic aviation corridors, driven by asymmetric fare movements across advance booking windows. While short-lead booking windows on primary business routes experienced noticeable upward price momentum, broader aggregate index inflation was moderated by price compression in longer-dated windows and stable pricing on major high-density trunk lines.

The upward trajectory in the overall index was primarily led by the Delhi–Bengaluru corridor (30% route weight), which posted a route-level APIx of 104.16 (+4.16%). This rise was propelled by sharp price spikes in near-term booking windows, most notably at the T+7 offset, where target median fares surged 11.02% to ₹9,558 (from a base of ₹8,609), and the T+1 offset, which rose 7.83% to ₹11,500.5. In contrast, the heavily weighted Delhi–Bombay route (40% weight) remained virtually flat with an APIx of 100.17 (+0.17%), as target medians across T+1, T+15, and T+7 held steady around ₹6,530. Meanwhile, the Calcutta–Bombay corridor (30% weight) acted as a disinflationary drag, recording an APIx of 98.08 (-1.92%). This contraction was driven by a steep 28.76% plummet in its T+45 window median—dropping to ₹9,201 from a base median of ₹12,915—which comfortably absorbed a 10.84% increase in the route's T+30 window median (to ₹10,129).

Granular flight-level scraping reveals notable carrier pricing strategies and structural shifts stemming from secondary airport infrastructure. On the Delhi–Bengaluru corridor, tight short-lead supply elevated non-stop fares, where the lowest T+1 non-stop flight started at ₹10,832 (IndiGo 6E-871), leaving 1-stop itineraries as the absolute floor at ₹10,077. Crucially, regional airport additions are introducing price arbitrage into the Delhi and Mumbai metropolitan catchment areas. For instance, Jewar Airport (DXN) yielded the lowest overall T+15 fare on the Delhi–Bombay path at ₹4,860 via Akasa Air (QP-1940), well below the ₹6,530 mainline DEL–BOM median. Similarly, low-cost carriers like Akasa Air and Air India Express aggressively undercut market medians—offering sub-₹8,400 fares on Calcutta–Bombay at T+1 and T+7, as well as sub-₹8,700 flights arriving into Navi Mumbai (NMI) at T+45—whereas market-leader IndiGo firmly defended price floors across prime non-stop trunk flights.

Looking ahead, domestic airfare pressures are expected to remain tightly segmented, characterized by persistent short-horizon fare volatility on high-yield commercial routes alongside discounting in extended booking windows. From a monetary policy standpoint, the localized price spikes on tech-hub corridors like Delhi–Bengaluru require ongoing monitoring for potential short-term spillovers into the transport service component of CPI inflation. However, the growing price divergence and lower fare floors introduced by secondary airport hubs (such as Jewar and Navi Mumbai) indicate an expanding structural capacity buffer, which should serve to anchored aggregate aviation services inflation over the medium-term policy horizon.
